title: Looking back to travel light: progenitor genomes empower hybrid potato breeding
content: “The longer you can look back, the farther you can look forward,” Winston Churchill once famously remarked. This quote rings especially true for breeding of potato (Solanum tuberosum). Unlike crops such as maize, in which breeders routinely cross elite inbred lines to exploit hybrid vigor, potato breeding still relies largely on highly heterozygous tetraploid plants propagated clonally via tubers (Li et al. 2013). This heterozygosity can mask deleterious variants, which are genetic changes at evolutionarily conserved sites predicted to reduce fitness (Wu et al. 2023). When developing homozygous diploid lines through repeated selfing, previously masked deleterious alleles can become homozygous and thus reduce vigor and yield. Thus, this heavy “genetic baggage” has become a major bottleneck for redesigning potato as a seed-propagated diploid crop for hybrid breeding. Although recent breeding has successfully purged many large-effect deleterious variants, existing inbred lines still carry numerous minor-effect variants, which collectively reduce their fitness and can compromise the performance of resulting hybrids (Zhang et al. 2021). Looking back at the domestication history of potato may reveal how the frequencies of these variants changed over time and help breeders “look forward” to the future of hybrid potato breeding.
